citation: Digital Promise. (2025). AI Literacy in PK-12 Education. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Six-domain AI skills and competencies framework for PK-12 learners
description: The brief presents PK-12 learner AI competencies across six domains: technical knowledge, practical implementation, ethical evaluation, analytical skills, interpersonal and communication skills, and adaptive skills. Sample competencies include "Using age-appropriate AI tools effectively for learning tasks" and cross-referencing AI outputs with reputable sources. The framework draws on EDSAFE AI Alliance, CSTA & AI4K12, ISTE, Kapor Foundation, and Mills et al. sources, and the brief stresses AI literacy builds on foundational digital competencies already embedded in PK-12 curricula rather than a new skill set from scratch.
requirements: Instruction must be developmentally appropriate for learners to meaningfully engage with the concepts
constraints: The field is still developing evidence-based recommendations for learner AI literacy
target_learning_goals: Understand, evaluate, and effectively use AI tools as appropriate across learning, work, and civic contexts
examples: Appendix D connects foundational skills such as early data literacy lessons to understanding how AI systems work and make decisions
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2025). AI Literacy in PK-12 Education. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/19fd2afb-0811-4e48-90d9-0ad6c9887a1a

article_title: Determining the degree of randomness in multiple-choice question distractors
citation: Diener, J. P. W., Frick, B. L., & Kriek, J. (2026). Determining the degree of randomness in multiple-choice question distractors. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01431
title: pK–D̄ quadrant classification: low randomness on a poorly answered question is the diagnostically rich case; high randomness is the null case
description: Items are plotted with percentage correct pK on one axis and scaled randomness D̄ on the other, forming four quadrants. Q3 (low pK, low D̄) signals the class converged on a shared, identifiable error and is the pattern most worth an instructor's attention; Q1 (high randomness) is the null case consistent with undifferentiated guessing. The paper states "The pedagogically consequential contrast is between Q1 and Q3", and Q2 and Q4 are of secondary interest because D̄ adds little there.
requirements: Calculation of pK and D̄ for every item from a single administration
constraints: The quadrant assignment is silent at the four-way boundary point; a caveat applies that uniform distributions do not prove guessing
target_learning_goals: identifying items warranting targeted re-teaching versus broader intervention
examples: In the FMCE application, most data points clustered in Q2 and Q3, consistent with the poor class scores
key_sources: Diener, J. P. W., Frick, B. L., & Kriek, J. (2026). Determining the degree of randomness in multiple-choice question distractors. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01431
